opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the core value proposition is pretty simple to state, even if it's subtle to execute well. Advertisers and publishers each hold data that's valuable in combination — an advertiser knows who bought their product, a publisher knows who saw which ads — but neither side wants to, or increasingly is allowed to, just hand their raw customer data over to the other. A clean room is meant to be a neutral environment where you can join those datasets and compute things like campaign reach, overlap, or conversion attribution without either party seeing the other's individual-level records.

Now, where it gets interesting from my perspective as someone who's worked on privacy for a long time is that "clean room" historically has been more of a contractual and access-control notion than a mathematical one. You put the data in a locked box, you restrict the queries people can run, maybe you impose minimum aggregation thresholds — don't report any count below fifty, say. And those are sensible heuristics, but we know from decades of research that aggregate statistics can leak individual information if you ask enough cleverly chosen questions. Differencing attacks are the classic example: ask for a count over a group, then the same group minus one person, and you've learned something about that person.

So the real opportunity, I think, is to put rigorous privacy guarantees underneath the clean room — differential privacy being the obvious candidate — so that the promise to consumers and to the data partners isn't just "we've restricted access," but "here is a provable bound on how much any single individual's data can influence what comes out." That lets you be quantitative about the trade-off between the accuracy advertisers need for measurement and the privacy protection you're giving people.

And I'd say the value is growing, not shrinking, because the old infrastructure — third-party cookies, cross-site tracking — is being dismantled by regulation and by the browser and platform companies. Advertisers still want to know whether their spend is working. Clean rooms, done carefully, are one of the more principled ways to keep answering that question without going back to the free-for-all of moving personal data around.

r001.rationale: The response says clean rooms keep raw data from being handed to the other party and restrict which queries can be run against it, communicating controlled access to the owner’s dataset.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what you mean by "value," and for whom.

The basic idea of a clean room is pretty simple. You have two parties, say an advertiser and a platform, each of whom has data about users, and each of whom has reasons, both legal and commercial, not to just hand that data over to the other. So you put the data in an environment where neither party can see the raw records of the other, and you only let out aggregate results, things like how many people who saw this campaign went on to make a purchase, that sort of thing.

So the value proposition is that you get the analytical benefit of combining the datasets without the exposure of actually sharing them. And I think that's genuinely useful. Attribution and measurement are real problems in advertising, and the old way of doing it, with third-party cookies and identifiers flowing all over the place, was a privacy disaster. Clean rooms are a step in a better direction.

But here's where I'd push back a bit, and this comes from the work I've done on differential privacy and privacy more broadly. "You can only see aggregates" is not actually a privacy guarantee. Aggregates can leak a lot. If I'm allowed to ask enough queries, or ask cleverly constructed ones, I can often reconstruct individual-level information from the answers. This is a well-understood phenomenon in the privacy literature, and it's exactly why differential privacy was invented. So the question I always ask about any particular clean room is, what are the actual technical controls? Is there noise added to the outputs? Are there limits on how many queries you can run, and are those limits principled or just a number somebody picked? Is there a formal privacy budget, or is it mostly contractual, where the guarantee is really "we promised not to misuse it"?

Many of the clean rooms in the market today are closer to the contractual end. They're access control plus some aggregation thresholds. That's not nothing, but it's not the same as a rigorous privacy guarantee, and I worry a little that the term "clean room" does some marketing work, suggesting a level of protection that the underlying mechanism doesn't necessarily deliver.

The other thing I'd say is that the real value is in forcing people to think about the question that matters, which is: what's the minimal thing you actually need to learn? Advertisers often think they need user-level data when what they really need is a handful of aggregate statistics about campaign effectiveness. If the clean room framing pushes people toward asking only the questions they need answered, and if those answers are delivered with real privacy protections, then I think they're a genuinely good development. If they just become a way of laundering the same old data-sharing practices under a more respectable name, then less so.

r001.rationale: The response says the parties’ data stay in an environment where neither can see the other’s raw records and only aggregate results are released, describing controlled access to each owner’s dataset.

astra-6.text:
I think the value is that they provide a controlled way for parties to learn something from their combined data without simply handing that data over to one another. In advertising, an advertiser and a platform might want to understand whether a campaign resulted in purchases. Answering that question can require connecting information that neither party has on its own.

But the important question is what the clean room allows you to compute and what it allows you to take out. Keeping the raw data inside a secure environment is useful, but it doesn’t automatically mean that the results you release preserve privacy. If you permit sufficiently detailed queries, or enough overlapping queries, those answers can reveal information about individuals.

So I see clean rooms as useful infrastructure. The privacy protection depends on the rules governing access and outputs, and that’s where something like differential privacy can play an important role. You want to enable useful aggregate measurement while putting a meaningful limit on what anyone can learn about a particular person.

r001.rationale: The response describes controlled collaboration and access rules, but does not clearly state that a data owner controls how another party accesses the owner's dataset.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value is that they let companies collaborate on data without simply handing their data over to one another. In advertising, you might have an advertiser that knows who purchased a product and a platform that knows who saw an ad. You’d like to understand the relationship between those things without either party revealing its entire customer database.

A clean room can provide a controlled environment for doing that analysis. But the privacy question doesn’t disappear just because you’ve put the data in a clean room. You still have to ask: What queries are allowed? What results can come out? Can someone combine those results to learn something about an individual? So I see clean rooms as useful infrastructure, but the strength of the privacy protection depends on the rules and mechanisms governing what leaves that environment.

r001.rationale: The response describes a controlled environment and rules governing queries and outputs, but does not clearly state that the data owner controls how the other party accesses the owner’s dataset.
